after.label: Complete extended journey
10. What does a gift make possible?
A wife shows her late husband’s keepsake ring
after.description: Zwingli’s own analogy: her words name the person recalled, not the ring’s material.

reading.attribution: Quotation — Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper (1526), Third Article; Bromiley 1953. An illustrative wife, not a documented widow at Marburg.

after.label: Zwingli: the ascended body awaits its return
after.description: His reading distinguishes the body’s departure from Christ’s continuing divine presence.

reading.text: Ascension concerns Christ’s humanity; divine presence need not mean his body is present in the meal.
reading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase — Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper (1526), Second Article. This is his contested interpretive rule.

after.label: Luther: bread and wine joined to Christ’s words
after.description: He retains bread and wine while affirming the body and blood through Christ’s institution.

reading.text: The Word must make a Sacrament of the element
reading.attribution: Quotation — Luther, Large Catechism V10 (1529), Bente/Dau 1921 translation.

after.label: An unbelieving guest eats at the instituted meal
after.description: Hypothetical application of Luther’s distinction between the sacrament and its saving benefit; not a reported Marburg incident.

after.label: Article 15 affirms spiritual reception of Christ’s body and blood
after.description: The shared affirmative clause of a jointly signed statement; examine its scope against the reconstructed arguments.

reading.text: Both sides affirm spiritual reception of Christ’s body and blood and a meal that strengthens faith.
reading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase — Marburg Articles 15, 3 October 1529; read as a limited agreement, not reconciliation.

after.label: The disputants pledge Christian love, as conscience permits
after.description: Article 15 attaches a duty of conduct to a disagreement it does not resolve.

after.label: A sign may carry the name of what it recalls
after.description: The ring makes figurative naming intelligible. It does not prove that the Supper’s words must be figurative.

after.label: Zwingli reads the meal as remembrance of the ascended body
after.description: The analogy supplies a possible reading; his ascension rule motivates choosing it. He does not deny Christ’s divine presence.

after.label: Presence does not settle whether bread’s substance remains
after.description: Aquinas affirms conversion of bread’s substance. Luther’s account retains bread; affirming Christ’s body does not identify these two explanations.

after.label: Luther and Zwingli retain bread; bodily presence divides them
after.description: Their shared material does not decide what is received: Luther affirms the body in the meal; Zwingli interprets its bread as a memorial sign.

after.label: They can sign spiritual reception without settling bodily presence
after.description: The shared clause does not erase the constructed disagreement. It records a narrower agreement, not a winner.

after.label: An unresolved quarrel does not cancel the claim to serve
after.description: Luther’s earlier service argument can support love despite disagreement. The signed pledge retains a conscience limit; it is not modern religious toleration.

after.label: For Luther, unbelief does not unmake the instituted sacrament
after.description: Its identity rests on Christ’s words rather than the guest’s virtue. Saving benefit still requires faith; validity is not a promise that every guest benefits.

reading.text: Its identity rests on Christ’s words rather than the guest’s virtue. Saving benefit still requires faith; validity is not a promise that every guest benefits.
reading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase — Luther, Large Catechism, Part V, §§16–18 and 33–37 (1529), Bente/Dau 1921 translation. Sacramental identity and benefit received through faith are distinguished.

after.label: Trent: grace calls and assists before any deserving
after.description: The council says that prior grace quickens and assists the adult’s response; it is not merely an earlier invitation.

reading.text: without any merits existing on their parts
reading.attribution: Quotation — Council of Trent, Session VI, chapter V (1547), Waterworth 1848.

after.label: The called adult can assent—or refuse
after.description: Trent’s adult preparation is a response, not inert reception.

after.label: Neither preceding faith nor works merit justification
after.description: ChapterVIII concerns the initial gift, not every later role of action.

after.label: Received justice can increase through grace-assisted works
after.description: Chapter VII includes inward renewal in justification; chapter X and canon 24 assign later works more than an evidential role.

after.label: Luther: the good tree bears fruit, not fruit the tree
after.description: A 1520 leaf returns to explain your earlier service manuscript.

reading.text: Good works do not make a good man, but a good man does good works
reading.attribution: Quotation — Luther, Concerning Christian Liberty (1520), Project Gutenberg public-domain translation. Compare this text, not a later Lutheran confession.

after.label: At Trent, grace enables a response it does not replace
after.description: Prior aid and the adult’s consent answer different questions. Augustine supplies a comparison, not proof of identical positions.

after.label: Required consent is not a price paid for justification
after.description: An enabled response need not merit the gift it receives.

after.label: Initial gift and growth in received justice are distinct
after.description: Denying prior merit does not deny every causal role to subsequent works.

after.label: Luther’s service follows righteousness rather than producing it
after.description: The tree analogy explains the direction of the earlier argument: faith frees the person to serve, not to seek justification through deeds.

after.label: Gifted grace leaves a dispute about what later works do
after.description: The 1520 text makes service flow from righteousness; Trent assigns works a role in increasing received justice. Neither premise here makes the initial gift a purchase. This contrast does not mean Luther denies growth in faith.

after.label: “This is my body”
after.description: The disputed words are quoted by both writers; repeating them does not decide their meaning.

reading.attribution: Short scriptural phrase quoted in Luther, Large Catechism V13, and Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper, Third Article; not an invented colloquy speech.

after: Optional continuation research v1 adds two isolated desks after finalized v10. Existing item/recipe/stage/source content is unchanged. New future uses intentionally retain earned manuscripts in this extended graph; this is not a claim of identical token retirement/layout before extension. Logical testing only; no publication, integration, UI or fresh-player evidence claimed. The desks are editorial manuscript arrangements, not literal historical meeting transcripts.

before: Across eight desks, build and question arguments about evil, freedom, bodies and grace. Manuscripts answer other manuscripts; agreement is not the same as victory. A completed argument reconstructs its author’s position, not a proof of belief.
after: Across ten manuscript desks, build and question arguments about evil, freedom, bodies and grace. Carry earlier arguments into new disputes, and discover what shared words and premises leave unresolved. A completed argument reconstructs a historical position; it does not prove a belief.

after.title: Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper (1526), Second and Third Articles
after.note: Primary text after THE TEXT; G. W. Bromiley, Zwingli and Bullinger (1953), pp.185–238. New readings are original paraphrases; six words of distinctive modern wording plus the shared four-word scriptural phrase are quoted. The editorial introduction is not Zwingli. Ring at Third Article; ascension/two natures at Second Article.

after.title: Luther, Large Catechism V, The Sacrament of the Altar (1529)
after.note: Bente/Dau 1921 public-domain translation; §§8–18 for bread, Word, and unworthy recipients; §§33–37 distinguish benefit received by faith. Do not substitute later Formula of Concord terminology.

after.title: The Marburg Articles, 3 October 1529, Articles 10 and 15
after.note: Primary joint statement, translated by Ellen Yutzy Glebe; original paraphrases only. Article 15 affirms spiritual reception, records corporal-presence disagreement, and qualifies mutual love by conscience. A signature is not doctrinal convergence.

after.title: Council of Trent, Session VI, Decree on Justification, 13 January 1547
after.note: J. Waterworth 1848 public-domain translation, pp.30–53. Chapters V–VIII and X; canon24. Distinguish grace-assisted adult preparation, unmerited initial justification, inward renewal, and increase of received justice. God is efficient cause, Christ meritorious, baptism instrumental, inward justice formal.

after.title: What can both sides sign?
after.speaker: Marburg arguments · 1526–1529 texts, with the agreement of 3 October 1529
after.motivation: A ring, an ascension text, a catechism and a signed article lie beside your earlier Aquinas and Luther manuscripts. Reconstruct why the same words permit different readings for these writers. Then find what their signatures can—and cannot—settle.
